In brief

Parody. "And whereas on the sixteenth day [...] preferred a charge against him for he was a malefactor": after J. J. O'Molloy, a lawyer, walks in, having been "round at the court," the talk in the bar turns to legal actions, and this mocking voice purports to describe things that have happened in two Dublin courtrooms on June 16. The paragraph's opening "And whereas" suggests that it is going to ape the language of legal documents, as in the chapter's first parody, but more than half of the prose revisits the vein of romanticized medieval nobility mined in the next half-dozen parodies and then revisited periodically throughout the chapter.

At more length

Legal language prevails several times: "Justice Andrews, sitting without a jury in the probate court, weighed well and pondered the claim of the first chargeant upon the property in the matter of the will propounded and final testamentary disposition in re the real and personal estate of the late lamented Jacob Halliday, vintner, deceased, versus Livingstone, an infant, of unsound mind, and another"; "they should well and truly try and true deliverance make in the issue joined between their sovereign lord the king and the prisoner at the bar and true verdict give according to the evidence so help them God and kiss the book"; "preferred a charge against him for he was a malefactor." But these echoes of actual courtroom expressions do little to advance the chapter's aim of monstrously inflating ordinary events. That task falls to the by-now-familiar strategy of turning contemporary Dubliners into heroic figures from Ireland's tribal past. As in some other parodies, phrases from biblical and Greco-Roman antiquity assist the elevation.

One of these occurs immediately. Calling this day "the sixteenth day of the month of the oxeyed goddess" recalls the epithet "ox-eyed" attached to Hera in the Iliad. Hera's Roman equivalent is Juno, and the Romans named the month of June after her, so it is the month of the oxeyed goddess. An astronomical detail follows: "the daughter of the skies, the virgin moon being then in her first quarter." The second phrase recalls the Greek and Roman identification of the moon with Artemis and Diana, virgin goddesses, but the first expression echoes Gaelic mythology. Harald Beck, John Simpson, and Ronan Crowley have noted on James Joyce Online Notes several places in which the language of Cyclops is indebted to James MacPherson's Poems of Ossian. One of those poems, Comala, exclaims, "Rise, moon, thou daughter of the sky!" In another, Fingal,  "Connal mounts the cars of gems. They stretch their shields, like darkened moon, the daughter of the starry skies, when she moves, a dun circle through heaven, and dreadful change expected by men."

Several sentences after these mythological scene-settings, people in the courtrooms undergo similar transformation into notables of antiquity. Sir Frederick Falkiner becomes "sir Frederick the Falconer"—evidently an eminent medieval huntsman. He sits "to administer the law of the brehons," an ancient Gaelic legal code. Brehon law (from the old Irish word for judge, breithim) was a largely oral but nevertheless sophisticated collection of civil statutes that governed daily Irish life. After the Norman invasion it operated alongside English common law for a long time, but in the 17th century it was finally supplanted.

The parody gives this old Gaelic tradition some biblical coloration when it describes the 12 members of the jury in Falkiner's case as "the high sinhedrim of the twelve tribes of Iar." The Great Sanhedrin, composed of 71 wise men who met in the Temple in Jerusalem, was the highest court and ruling council in ancient Israel (there were also lesser Sanhedrin of 23 judges in each city). Iar is an Irish word that can mean west or western, so it refers to Ireland.

Not in the least concerned with consistency, the parody makes the jury members modern avatars not only of the 71 judges of the Sanhedrin but also of the Twelve Tribes of Israel. It keeps things local by replacing the biblical names (Reuben, Simeon, Levi, Judah, Dan, Naphtali, Gad, Asher, Issachar, Zebulun, Joseph, Benjamin) with Irish ones (Patrick, Hugh, Owen, Conn, Oscar, Fergus, Finn, Dermot, Cormac, Kevin, Caolte, Ossian), noting that "for every tribe one man" sat on the jury. All twelve names evoke great Irish leaders of the medieval past—kings, warriors of the Fianna, holy men, the poet Ossian—though some of them could refer to several such personages. In this list, as in the lists of the contents of the produce markets, one confronts both Cyclopean forms of gigantism: the exaggeration of ennoblement and the exaggeration of exhaustive cataloguing.

The paragraph ends with the judge swearing in the members of the jury and a defendant being arraigned. Here the prose liberally sprinkles in medieval-sounding vocabulary. God becomes "Him who died on rood" (the Old and Middle English word for a cross), "Him who is from everlasting," "His rightwiseness." Officers of the court become "the minions of the law," their jail cell a "donjon keep" (two synonymous medieval terms for the heavily fortified center of a castle), the defendant a man arrested by "the sleuthhounds of justice," and the refusal of bail "ne bail ne mainprise" ("ne...ne" means "neither...nor" in Middle English, and mainprise was the practice of entrusting a prisoner to someone who promised to produce him in court at a later date).

By this point in Cyclops readers too may be feeling the weary impatience with a Noble Medieval Past that afflicted Joyce as he waded through the patriotic waters of the Irish Literary Revival.

John Hunt 2026
